fact: Human Rights Watch reports that Niger's 2019 cybercrime law, amended by the junta in 2024 to restore prison terms of up to five years and fines for disseminating data likely to disturb public order, was the law under which charges were brought in October 2025.

Per Human Rights Watch, police in Niamey arrested six journalists on 30 October 2025 and the authorities charged them with complicity in disseminating a document likely to disturb public order under the 2019 cybercrime law, for sharing an invitation to a state press conference; three were detained at Kollo prison. The law was used against journalists.
Human Rights Watch says a Niamey prosecutor charged lawyer Abrourahamane Lirwana with spreading data likely to disturb public order under Niger's cybercrime law, which shows the law is in force.

Human Rights Watch says Lirwana was charged under the cybercrime law and detained from 21 September 2026, with prosecutors seeking five years at a 6 October hearing, and that the junta has detained journalists under it.
Le Sahel reports Niger's law no. 2019-33 of 3 July 2019 on the repression of cybercrime, significantly amended on 12 June 2024 to set penalties for online defamation, insults and harmful data.

fact: EU SEE (Hivos) reports that on 13 October 2026 the Niamey High Court of First Instance convicted lawyer Lirwana Abdourahmane, prosecuted under Article 31 of the law on cybercrime over a social media post, and sentenced him to two years unsuspended and a 2 million CFA franc fine.
EU SEE (Hivos) reports a Niamey court convicted a lawyer under Article 31 of Niger's law on cybercrime on 13 October 2026, showing the law is applied.

Niger's judicial police cybercrime division arrested suspects in three September 2026 cases of electronic fraud, blackmail and illegal access to Niger Telecom accounts, all referred to the prosecutor between 1 and 24 September 2026.
